extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students taking a first course in proofs and elementary set theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and evaluating elementary mathematical proofs (direct, contrapositive, contradiction), biconditional and existence proofs, and basic proofs about sets (membership, subset, equality, operations). Targets students preparing solutions to textbook exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct/contrapositive over contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite the power of proof by contradiction, it's best to use it only when the direct and contrapositive approaches do not seem to work. The reason for this is that a proof by contradiction can often have hidden in it a simpler contrapositive proof, and if this is the case it's better to go with the simpler approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contradiction sparingly; if a contradiction proof essentially assumes the negation of the conclusion and deduces the negation of the hypothesis, you are doing a contrapositive proof and should rewrite it as such for clarity and efficiency. Example given: a^2 - 2a + 7 even implies a odd — contrapositive is cleaner than a contradiction that hides a contrapositive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for If-And-Only-If (biconditional) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'P if and only if Q' you must prove both conditional statements: If P then Q, and If Q then P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove P => Q and then prove Q => P (each may use direct, contrapositive, or contradiction). Always begin a new paragraph for the converse (Q => P) and commonly begin that paragraph with 'Conversely' to signal the switch and remind the reader which statement is being proved. Example: prove n odd <=> n^2 odd by showing each direction separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove equivalence of multiple statements via implication chains
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that a list of statements are equivalent, prove conditional implications linking them so that truth of one forces truth of all (a circular chain suffices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One efficient scheme is to prove (a) => (b) => (c) => ... => (a) giving a circular pattern; this minimizes the number of conditional statements required. Other patterns are valid but may require more implications. Each conditional may be proved by direct, contrapositive, or contradiction proof. Example: six equivalent statements about invertibility of an n×n matrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs by example
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an existential statement ∃x R(x), provide a specific example x0 and verify R(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display and verify a concrete object that satisfies the property. Examples: 'There exists an even prime' demonstrated by 2; 'There exists an integer expressible as sum of two cubes in two ways' demonstrated by 1729 (with explicit equalities). WARNING: an example proves an existence statement but does not prove a universal conditional statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show membership a ∈ {x : P(x)} and a ∈ {x ∈ S : P(x)}
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a ∈ {x : P(x)} show that P(a) is true. To show a ∈ {x ∈ S : P(x)} verify both a ∈ S and P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definition-of-set-builder approach: the set consists of exactly those x making P(x) true (and lying in S if specified). Many examples illustrate checking both components when S is explicit (e.g., A = {x ∈ N : 7 | x}).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove A ⊆ B (standard approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⊆ B show that every element of A is an element of B, i.e., show the conditional 'If x ∈ A then x ∈ B'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct approach: assume x ∈ A and deduce x ∈ B (this usually yields the most straightforward proof). Contrapositive approach: prove the contrapositive 'If x ∉ B then x ∉ A' by assuming x ∉ B and deducing x ∉ A. Contradiction can also be used: assume x ∈ A and x ∉ B and derive a contradiction. Numerous examples (divisibility, congruence, intersections) illustrate both approaches and choice-of-method guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equality of sets A = B
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard procedure to prove A = B is to prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show each subset inclusion separately; once both directions are established, conclude A = B. Examples include proving {n : 35 | n} = {n : 5 | n} ∩ {n : 7 | n} by proving the two inclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equalities by mutual inclusion or algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: You may prove an identity of sets by showing mutual subset inclusion (two inclusions) or by manipulating set-builder expressions into identical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, perform stepwise algebraic/logical equalities on set-builder descriptions to transform one side to the other; this can shorten proofs but may be harder to apply. Example: A×(B∩C) = (A×B) ∩ (A×C) proved both by mutual inclusion and by algebraic manipulation of predicate forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cartesian product to deduce set equality when product factor nonempty
rubrics_metrics.description: If C ≠ ∅ and A × C = B × C, then A = B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: for any a ∈ A pick c ∈ C to get (a,c) ∈ A×C = B×C, hence a ∈ B; reverse the roles to get B ⊆ A. This is a standard trick using existence of an element in the second factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set inclusion implies subset inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If 𝒫(A) ⊆ 𝒫(B) (power set inclusion) then A ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: for any a ∈ A consider the singleton {a} which is in 𝒫(A); by inclusion {a} ∈ 𝒫(B), so {a} ⊆ B and therefore a ∈ B. Use singleton-subset trick to move from power-set statements to element-level statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case analysis when proving statements about unions or unions of power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving X ∈ 𝒫(A) ∪ 𝒫(B) implies X ∈ 𝒫(A ∪ B), consider cases X ∈ 𝒫(A) and X ∈ 𝒫(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the definition of union and the definition of power set, handle each case separately, and observe overlapping cases are covered. The textbook gives the concrete example 𝒫(A) ∪ 𝒫(B) ⊆ 𝒫(A ∪ B) with case-based reasoning.
